19	**[Section 1 --- Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**
20	
21	**[1.1 Purpose]{.underline}**
22	
23	This Joint Defense Agreement Playbook (this \"Playbook\") establishes Vantage Industrial Solutions, Inc.\'s (\"Vantage\" or the \"Company\") uniform internal standards governing the review, evaluation, negotiation, and approval of any proposed joint defense agreement (\"JDA\") to which Vantage is asked to become a signatory. Joint defense agreements are a critical litigation tool that, when properly structured, preserve the common-interest privilege and facilitate the efficient sharing of information among co-defendants facing common claims. However, poorly drafted or inadequately negotiated JDAs can erode the Company\'s litigation posture, compromise privilege positions, restrict settlement flexibility, expose the Company to regulatory liability, and create conflicts of interest that impair long-term strategic planning.
24	
25	This Playbook is designed to protect Vantage\'s litigation posture, privilege positions, settlement flexibility, and regulatory compliance interests across all matters in which a JDA is contemplated. It provides a structured analytical framework that ensures consistent evaluation of JDA terms regardless of the specific matter, outside counsel engagement, or business unit involved. By establishing clear standards --- categorized as Required, Preferred, and Prohibited --- this Playbook enables outside counsel and in-house attorneys to identify material risks in proposed JDA provisions, negotiate toward acceptable terms, and document the basis for any departures from the Company\'s preferred positions.
26	
27	This Playbook is not intended to serve as a form JDA or to replace the exercise of professional judgment by qualified counsel. Rather, it sets the minimum floor and maximum ceiling for negotiating positions and provides the analytical rubric against which all proposed JDAs must be measured before Vantage will consider execution.
28	
29	**[1.2 Applicability]{.underline}**
30	
31	This Playbook applies to all JDAs --- whether styled as \"joint defense agreements,\" \"common interest agreements,\" \"joint prosecution agreements,\" \"mutual defense arrangements,\" or any functionally equivalent instrument --- in the following categories of proceedings:
32	
33	> • Federal and state civil litigation, including antitrust, product liability, commercial, environmental, securities, and intellectual property matters;
34	>
35	> • Multi-defendant regulatory proceedings before federal agencies (including, without limitation, the Department of Justice, the Federal Trade Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Environmental Protection Agency) and state-level agencies;
36	>
37	> • Related government investigations, including grand jury proceedings, civil investigative demand processes, and informal investigative inquiries; and
38	>
39	> • Any proceeding or pre-litigation matter in which Vantage\'s counsel determines that a common-interest arrangement with one or more third parties may be appropriate.
40	
41	All outside counsel retained by Vantage on any matter must review any proposed JDA against this Playbook before recommending execution. This obligation applies regardless of whether the proposed JDA originates from a co-defendant, co-defendant\'s counsel, a court-appointed liaison, or any other source. Outside counsel are expected to maintain familiarity with the current version of this Playbook and to confirm with the Office of the General Counsel that they are referencing the most recently issued version before undertaking any JDA review.
42	
43	This Playbook also applies to amendments, supplements, joinders, or modifications of existing JDAs to which Vantage is already a party. Any proposed change to an existing JDA must be evaluated under the same standards and approval process set forth herein.
44	
45	**[1.3 Obligation to Consult]{.underline}**
46	
47	No JDA may be executed on behalf of Vantage without the prior written approval of the General Counsel or his designee. This restriction applies without exception, regardless of the perceived urgency of the matter, the number of co-defendants involved, or the identity of the party proposing the JDA.
48	
49	Before seeking approval, outside counsel must prepare a written assessment of the proposed JDA measured against the standards set forth in this Playbook, as more fully described in Section 16 below. Oral approvals, email approvals not accompanied by the required written assessment, and approvals obtained from persons other than the General Counsel or a duly designated officer are not effective and do not authorize execution.
50	
51	Any officer, employee, or agent of Vantage who becomes aware that a JDA has been executed on the Company\'s behalf without proper approval must immediately notify the Office of the General Counsel.
52	
53	**[Section 2 --- Classification Framework]{.underline}**
54	
55	**[2.1 Three-Tier Classification]{.underline}**
56	
57	Each substantive JDA topic addressed in this Playbook is assigned one of three classification tiers. These tiers determine the degree of negotiating flexibility available to Vantage\'s counsel and the procedural requirements applicable to any departure from the stated standard.
58	
59	> **(a) Required.** Terms that must be included in any JDA Vantage executes, or minimum/maximum thresholds that must be satisfied. A \"Required\" classification denotes that the standard reflects a non-negotiable element of Vantage\'s JDA position --- one that the Office of the General Counsel has determined is necessary to protect the Company\'s core interests. A proposed JDA that does not satisfy a Required standard may not be executed unless the General Counsel grants a written exception documenting the business justification and the associated risk. Written exceptions are granted sparingly and are maintained in a confidential exception log by the Office of the General Counsel.
60	>
61	> **(b) Preferred.** Terms representing Vantage\'s recommended negotiating position. A \"Preferred\" classification indicates that the standard reflects best practices and the Company\'s optimal outcome, but that departure is permissible where a reasonable alternative is obtained through good-faith negotiation. Any departure from a Preferred standard must be noted and explained in the review memorandum provided to the General Counsel. The review memorandum should identify the specific Preferred standard, the proposed alternative, the reason the counterparty is unwilling to accept the Preferred position, and an assessment of the risk associated with the departure.
62	>
63	> **(c) Prohibited (\"Never Accept\").** Terms that Vantage will not agree to under any circumstances. A \"Prohibited\" classification denotes a provision that poses unacceptable risk to the Company\'s interests and for which no business justification can overcome the associated exposure. No exception process is available for Prohibited terms. A proposed JDA containing a Prohibited term must be redlined to remove or replace it as a condition of execution. If a counterparty refuses to remove a Prohibited term, Vantage will not execute the JDA.
64	
65	**[2.2 Structure of Each Topic Section]{.underline}**
66	
67	For each topic covered in Sections 3 through 14 of this Playbook, the discussion follows a uniform structure designed to facilitate efficient review by both outside counsel and in-house attorneys:
68	
69	> \(i\) **Classification Tier** --- identifying the applicable tier (Required, Preferred, or Prohibited);
70	>
71	> \(ii\) **Acceptable Position** --- stating the term or threshold that satisfies the applicable standard;
72	>
73	> \(iii\) **Fallback Positions** --- describing any permissible alternative positions that Vantage may accept if the primary acceptable position is not obtainable through negotiation; and
74	>
75	> \(iv\) **Never-Accept Terms** --- where applicable, identifying the corresponding Prohibited terms that must be rejected, including illustrative formulations commonly encountered in proposed JDAs.
76	
77	This structure ensures that outside counsel can quickly locate the applicable standard, assess whether a proposed provision satisfies or departs from it, and identify any Prohibited terms that may be embedded within otherwise acceptable language.
78	
79	**[2.3 Interaction Among Tiers]{.underline}**
80	
81	It is important to recognize that a single JDA provision may implicate both a Required standard and a corresponding Prohibited standard. For example, a settlement-notice provision may include an acceptable notice period (satisfying a Required standard) while simultaneously requiring disclosure of material settlement terms (a Prohibited term). Both dimensions of the provision must be evaluated; satisfaction of the Required standard does not excuse the presence of a Prohibited term within the same provision.
82	
83	Outside counsel must read each provision of a proposed JDA holistically, cross-referencing the relevant sections of this Playbook, to ensure that all applicable standards --- Required, Preferred, and Prohibited --- are addressed. The written assessment submitted to the General Counsel must reflect this comprehensive analysis.
84	
85	**[Section 3 --- Withdrawal Rights]{.underline}**
86	
87	**Classification: Required**
88	
89	**[3.1 Acceptable Position]{.underline}**
90	
91	Vantage must retain an unconditional right to withdraw from any JDA upon written notice to all other parties. The required notice period shall be no more than **fifteen (15) calendar days** from the date written notice of withdrawal is delivered to the other signatories.
92	
93	The withdrawal right must be unconditional, meaning that it may not be contingent upon the occurrence of any triggering event, the consent of any other party, a vote of the Steering Committee, or any other precondition. Vantage must be free to withdraw for any reason or no reason, at any time, by providing the prescribed written notice.
94	
95	**Rationale:** An unconditional withdrawal right with a short notice period preserves Vantage\'s ability to pivot its litigation strategy, pursue independent settlement discussions, respond to changed circumstances in government investigations, or otherwise adjust its posture without being locked into a joint defense arrangement that no longer serves the Company\'s interests. Extended notice periods or conditional withdrawal mechanisms create a risk that co-defendants will use the notice window to take strategic actions that prejudice Vantage\'s position, including accelerating discovery sharing, altering joint briefing strategies, or communicating settlement-related information to adverse parties.
96	
97	**[3.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
98	
99	If a counterparty proposes a notice period exceeding fifteen (15) calendar days, Vantage\'s counsel should negotiate to reduce the period to fifteen (15) calendar days. There is no permissible fallback above the fifteen-calendar-day ceiling. Outside counsel may not accept a withdrawal-notice period of sixteen (16) calendar days or more, regardless of the business justification offered by the counterparty.
100	
101	In the event that the proposed JDA conditions the right of withdrawal on the approval of other signatories, a supermajority vote, or any similar mechanism, Vantage\'s counsel must redline the provision to restore an unconditional withdrawal right. Conditional withdrawal mechanisms are inconsistent with the Required standard and must be treated as a failure to satisfy this Section 3.
102	
103	**[3.3 Treatment of Shared Materials Upon Withdrawal]{.underline}**
104	
105	The JDA must provide that a withdrawing party has **no obligation to return or destroy materials that have already been reviewed and incorporated into that party\'s work product**. This is an essential corollary to the withdrawal right, because the practical value of withdrawal is substantially diminished if the withdrawing party must dismantle or reconstruct its litigation preparation upon departure from the joint defense arrangement.
106	
107	Any return-or-destroy obligation included in the JDA may apply only to materials in their original shared form that have not been reviewed and incorporated into the withdrawing party\'s work product. The JDA should define \"incorporation into work product\" broadly to include any use of shared materials in the preparation of pleadings, briefs, expert reports, deposition outlines, internal memoranda, or other litigation-related documents.
108	
109	**Rationale:** Requiring destruction of materials that have been incorporated into work product is impractical, as the substance of those materials will already be reflected in the withdrawing party\'s case preparation. Moreover, a blanket return-or-destroy obligation creates an unreasonable deterrent to withdrawal, because a party contemplating withdrawal would face the prospect of significantly impairing its own litigation position. This outcome is contrary to the policy underlying the withdrawal right and could be used by co-defendants to exert improper leverage over a party considering withdrawal.
110	
111	**[3.4 Never-Accept Term]{.underline}**
112	
113	The following terms are classified as Prohibited and must be rejected in any proposed JDA:
114	
115	> • Any withdrawal provision requiring notice exceeding fifteen (15) calendar days;
116	>
117	> • Any withdrawal provision conditioning the right of withdrawal on the consent or approval of other signatories, a Steering Committee vote, or any other precondition;
118	>
119	> • Any withdrawal provision imposing a blanket return-or-destroy obligation covering work-product-incorporated materials, including provisions requiring a withdrawing party to \"return or destroy all Joint Defense Materials\" without an express carve-out for materials incorporated into work product.
120	
121	**[Section 4 --- Settlement Notice]{.underline}**
122	
123	**Classification: Required and Prohibited (dual classification)**
124	
125	**[4.1 Acceptable Position --- Notice Timing (Required)]{.underline}**
126	
127	A settling party\'s obligation to notify other JDA members of its intent to settle must require no more than **ten (10) business days\' advance written notice** prior to the execution of a settlement agreement. The notice obligation should be triggered by the settling party\'s determination that it intends to proceed with a proposed settlement, not by the commencement of settlement discussions or the receipt of a settlement demand.
128	
129	**Rationale:** Longer notice windows risk interference with settlement negotiations, potential leaks of settlement information to plaintiffs or the market, and strategic manipulation by non-settling co-defendants who may use the extended notice period to take actions designed to obstruct or complicate the settling party\'s negotiations. The ten-business-day window provides adequate time for non-settling defendants to evaluate the impact of the proposed settlement on the joint defense without unduly burdening the settling party\'s ability to conclude its negotiations.
130	
131	**[4.2 Scope of Disclosure (Required)]{.underline}**
132	
133	Notice of intent to settle must be limited to the **existence and general nature** of the proposed settlement. Specifically, the settling party should be required to disclose only:
134	
135	> \(a\) The fact that it intends to enter into a settlement of claims in the underlying litigation;
136	>
137	> \(b\) The general nature of the settlement (e.g., full settlement of all claims against the settling party, partial settlement of specified claims, or settlement with identified plaintiff classes or groups); and
138	>
139	> \(c\) The anticipated timeline for execution and submission to the court for approval, if applicable.
140	
141	The JDA must not require disclosure of specific financial terms, the scope of releases, cooperation commitments, admissions or denials of liability, or any other material terms of the proposed settlement beyond what is described above.
142	
143	**Rationale:** The purpose of the settlement-notice obligation is to inform co-defendants that the joint defense arrangement is about to change --- not to provide co-defendants with a veto power or tactical advantage. Limiting disclosure to existence and general nature protects the settling party\'s negotiating position, preserves the confidentiality of settlement communications, and reduces the risk that co-defendants will attempt to use settlement information for strategic purposes adverse to the settling party\'s interests.
144	
145	**[4.3 Fallback Positions]{.underline}**
146	
147	> **(a) Timing.** Vantage may accept a notice period of up to ten (10) business days but not beyond. If a counterparty proposes a notice period exceeding ten (10) business days, outside counsel must negotiate to reduce it. There is no permissible fallback above the ten-business-day ceiling.
148	>
149	> **(b) Scope of Disclosure.** The \"existence and general nature\" limitation is non-negotiable. No fallback permitting broader disclosure is available. Outside counsel may not agree to any formulation that would require the settling party to disclose information beyond existence and general nature, regardless of the characterization used (e.g., \"summary terms,\" \"principal provisions,\" \"key elements\").
150	
151	**[4.4 Prohibited --- Disclosure of Material Settlement Terms]{.underline}**
152	
153	Any provision requiring a settling party to disclose **\"all material terms\"** of a proposed settlement to non-settling defendants is a **never-accept term**. This prohibition extends to all formulations that would require disclosure beyond existence and general nature, including but not limited to the following commonly encountered formulations:
154	
155	> • \"material financial terms\"
156	>
157	> • \"principal terms and conditions\"
158	>
159	> • \"key terms\"
160	>
161	> • \"material terms, including any cooperation obligations\"
162	>
163	> • \"the amount and structure of the settlement consideration\"
164	>
165	> • \"the scope of releases and cooperation commitments\"
166	>
167	> • Any language requiring the settling party to provide a copy, summary, or term sheet of the proposed settlement agreement to non-settling defendants
168	
169	**Rationale:** Disclosure of material settlement terms to co-defendants creates multiple categories of risk. First, co-defendants may use the information to obstruct or interfere with the settlement, including by threatening to withdraw from the JDA, altering joint defense strategy, or communicating directly with plaintiffs. Second, disclosure of financial terms may cause competitive harm if the co-defendants include competitors of the settling party. Third, disclosure of cooperation commitments may chill future settlement negotiations in the same or related matters. Fourth, requiring disclosure of settlement terms may result in waiver of the settlement-communication privilege recognized in many jurisdictions, potentially exposing privileged settlement negotiations to discovery by plaintiffs or other third parties.
170	
171	**[Section 5 --- Surviving Obligations (Confidentiality Duration)]{.underline}**
172	
173	**Classification: Required**
174	
175	**[5.1 Acceptable Position]{.underline}**
176	
177	Confidentiality obligations governing Joint Defense Materials --- including all documents, communications, analyses, memoranda, attorney work product, and other information shared among the parties pursuant to the JDA --- must survive termination of or withdrawal from the JDA. Vantage\'s preferred position is that the confidentiality obligations survive **indefinitely**, meaning that they continue in effect without any temporal limitation for so long as the materials remain privileged or confidential.
178	
179	Alternatively, if an indefinite survival provision is not obtainable, the JDA must provide for a defined survival period of **no fewer than seven (7) years** from the effective date of termination of the JDA or, in the case of a withdrawing party, from the effective date of that party\'s withdrawal.
180	
181	**[5.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
182	
183	Where a counterparty insists on a finite term for surviving confidentiality obligations, the minimum acceptable duration is seven (7) years from the effective date of termination or withdrawal. Vantage\'s preferred position remains indefinite survival, and outside counsel should advocate for indefinite survival as the primary negotiating position before agreeing to the seven-year alternative.
184	
185	If a counterparty proposes a survival period shorter than seven (7) years, outside counsel must negotiate upward. There is no permissible fallback below the seven-year floor.
186	
187	**[5.3 Never-Accept Term]{.underline}**
188	
189	Any surviving-obligations period shorter than seven (7) years from the effective date of termination or withdrawal is a never-accept term and must be rejected.
190	
191	**Rationale:** The litigation and regulatory landscape in which Vantage operates --- particularly in antitrust and environmental matters --- frequently involves follow-on proceedings, contribution actions, indemnification disputes, government investigations, and class-action opt-out litigation that may commence or continue well beyond the conclusion of the initial matter in which the JDA was formed. The applicable statutes of limitation and repose in these areas can extend to four years (federal antitrust), six years (state contract claims), or longer. A short survival period --- for example, two or three years --- creates a meaningful risk that the confidentiality protections will lapse while related proceedings remain pending, exposing shared privileged materials to discovery, subpoena, or compelled production in subsequent proceedings. The seven-year floor provides a reasonable margin of protection against this risk while remaining commercially reasonable.
192	
193	**[Section 6 --- Conflicts Waiver]{.underline}**
194	
195	**Classification: Required and Prohibited (dual classification)**
196	
197	**[6.1 Acceptable Position (Required)]{.underline}**
198	
199	Many JDAs contain provisions addressing the conflicts of interest that may arise from the participation of multiple parties --- and their respective counsel --- in a joint defense arrangement. Where the JDA contains any waiver of conflicts of interest arising from joint defense participation, the waiver must include an **express carve-out preserving each party\'s right to assert claims against any other JDA member in future litigation**, including but not limited to the following categories of claims:
200	
201	> \(a\) Claims for contribution;
202	>
203	> \(b\) Claims for contractual or equitable indemnity;
204	>
205	> \(c\) Cross-claims and counterclaims;
206	>
207	> \(d\) Third-party claims;
208	>
209	> \(e\) Claims arising under separate contractual relationships among the JDA members; and
210	>
211	> \(f\) Any other claim that one JDA member may have or acquire against another JDA member, whether arising out of or relating to the same underlying litigation or arising from separate transactions or occurrences.
212	
213	The carve-out must apply regardless of whether the future proceeding arises out of or relates to the same underlying litigation in which the JDA was formed. This is essential because contribution, indemnity, and cross-claim rights may not ripen until after judgment or settlement in the underlying action, and the scope of future disputes among JDA members cannot be predicted at the time of JDA execution.
214	
215	**[6.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
216	
217	The specific language of the carve-out may be negotiated in form, provided that the substance of each party\'s right to pursue inter-party claims is preserved. Alternative formulations are acceptable so long as they clearly and unambiguously reserve the right of each JDA member to assert any claim against any other JDA member in any future proceeding.
218	
219	An acceptable alternative to a carve-out is the **omission of any conflicts waiver entirely** --- that is, a JDA that contains no waiver-of-conflicts provision at all. This approach is preferable to a waiver without adequate carve-outs, as it avoids the risk that a broadly worded waiver will be construed to preclude inter-party claims.
220	
221	**[6.3 Prohibited --- Blanket Conflicts Waiver]{.underline}**
222	
223	A conflicts waiver with **no carve-out for future inter-party disputes** is a **never-accept term**. This prohibition applies to the following formulations, among others:
224	
225	> • Waivers that are silent on future adverse proceedings among JDA members;
226	>
227	> • Waivers that purport to waive conflicts \"without limitation\" or \"for all purposes\";
228	>
229	> • Waivers that state that each party \"waives any conflict of interest arising from participation in the joint defense\" without expressly reserving the right to assert future claims;
230	>
231	> • Waivers that include a release of claims among the signatories, whether express or implied; and
232	>
233	> • Waivers that condition future inter-party claims on the consent of other signatories or the Steering Committee.
234	
235	**Rationale:** A blanket conflicts waiver could be construed --- by a court, by opposing counsel, or by a co-defendant --- to preclude Vantage from asserting indemnification, contribution, or other cross-claims against co-defendants. Such an interpretation would materially impair Vantage\'s litigation flexibility and its ability to allocate fault in post-judgment or post-settlement proceedings. In multi-defendant antitrust and product-liability litigation, the right to pursue contribution and indemnity claims against co-defendants is a critical component of the Company\'s overall litigation strategy and risk management. A blanket waiver that extinguishes or arguably limits these rights is categorically unacceptable.
236	
237	**[Section 7 --- Governing Law]{.underline}**
238	
239	**Classification: Required**
240	
241	**[7.1 Acceptable Position]{.underline}**
242	
243	The governing law of the JDA must be **the law of the state where the underlying litigation is pending**. The choice-of-law provision should expressly identify the applicable state\'s substantive law, including its common-law and statutory rules governing privilege, contract interpretation, and the enforceability of joint defense and common-interest agreements.
244	
245	The choice-of-law provision should not disclaim the application of conflicts-of-law principles unless doing so is consistent with selecting the forum state\'s law. In most cases, a standard formulation providing that the JDA \"shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of \[Forum State\], without regard to its conflicts-of-law principles\" is acceptable, because the result --- application of forum-state law --- is the desired outcome.
246	
247	**Application Note:** Where the underlying litigation is pending in federal court in the Northern District of Illinois, the JDA must be governed by Illinois law. Where the underlying litigation is pending in state court in Texas, the JDA must be governed by Texas law.
248	
249	**[7.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
250	
251	If multiple related proceedings are pending in different jurisdictions --- for example, a federal MDL consolidated in one district and related state-court proceedings in another --- the governing law should be that of the forum in which the principal or lead case is pending. For purposes of this Playbook, the \"principal or lead case\" is the case designated as the lead case in an MDL proceeding, the case in which the most significant discovery is being conducted, or, if neither of these factors is dispositive, the case identified by the Steering Committee or by agreement of the parties as the lead case.
252	
253	Vantage will not accept governing law of a jurisdiction unrelated to the underlying litigation. Outside counsel must reject any proposed governing-law provision that selects a state in which no party is domiciled, no relevant conduct occurred, and no underlying proceeding is pending.
254	
255	**[7.3 Never-Accept Term]{.underline}**
256	
257	Selection of the governing law of a state with no nexus to the forum of the underlying proceeding is a never-accept term. For example, selection of New York law where the underlying litigation is pending exclusively in Illinois, and no party is domiciled in or has a principal place of business in New York, must be rejected.
258	
259	**Rationale:** The governing law of the JDA directly affects its enforceability, the scope and application of the common-interest privilege, the interpretation of contractual provisions, and the available remedies for breach. Selecting the law of the state where the underlying litigation is pending ensures that these issues are assessed under the legal framework most relevant to the pending case and most familiar to the presiding court. Selecting the law of an unrelated jurisdiction creates a risk of unpredictable results, including the possibility that the JDA will be interpreted under privilege standards that differ from those applied by the court in the underlying case, potentially undermining the privilege protections the JDA is designed to create.
260	
261	**[Section 8 --- Inadvertent Disclosure / Clawback]{.underline}**
262	
263	**Classification: Required**
264	
265	**[8.1 Acceptable Position]{.underline}**
266	
267	The JDA must include a clawback provision addressing the inadvertent disclosure of privileged or work-product-protected Joint Defense Materials. The acceptable formulation takes one of two forms:
268	
269	> **(a) Federal Rule of Evidence 502(d) Court Order.** The preferred approach is for the JDA to include a provision pursuant to which the parties agree to jointly seek a court order under Federal Rule of Evidence 502(d) providing that inadvertent disclosure of privileged or work-product-protected Joint Defense Materials does not constitute a waiver of the applicable privilege or protection, regardless of whether the disclosure is made in the underlying litigation, in related proceedings, or to any third party. A Rule 502(d) order is the gold standard because it provides protection that is binding on non-parties and in subsequent proceedings, as expressly provided by Rule 502(d).
270	>
271	> **(b) Contractual Clawback Mechanism.** Alternatively, the JDA may include a contractual clawback provision providing that inadvertent disclosure of privileged or work-product-protected Joint Defense Materials to third parties or in discovery does not waive the applicable privilege or work-product protection. The contractual clawback must obligate all parties --- including the receiving party, the disclosing party, and all other JDA members --- to take the following actions promptly upon notice of an inadvertent disclosure:
272	>
273	> \(i\) The disclosing party must notify all JDA members of the inadvertent disclosure promptly upon discovery;
274	>
275	> \(ii\) The receiving party (i.e., the non-JDA party that received the inadvertently disclosed materials) must be notified and requested to return, sequester, or destroy the materials;
276	>
277	> \(iii\) All JDA members must cooperate in seeking any available judicial relief to protect the privilege, including motions to compel return of the materials and protective orders; and
278	>
279	> \(iv\) No JDA member may use or rely upon another member\'s inadvertently disclosed privileged materials in any proceeding adverse to the disclosing member.
280	
281	**[8.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
282	
283	Where a court order under Rule 502(d) is not obtainable --- for example, because the underlying case is pending in state court in a jurisdiction that has not adopted an equivalent rule, or because the presiding judge declines to enter such an order --- the contractual clawback mechanism described in Section 8.1(b) above is the minimum acceptable alternative.
284

**[8.3 Never-Accept Term]{.underline}**

Omission of any clawback or inadvertent-disclosure mechanism from the JDA is a never-accept term. A proposed JDA that does not address inadvertent disclosure in any form must be redlined to include either a Rule 502(d) provision or a contractual clawback before Vantage will consider execution.

**Rationale:** Without clawback protection, an inadvertent production of shared Joint Defense Materials in discovery could result in subject-matter waiver of privilege across all JDA members. Under the prevailing standard in many jurisdictions, an inadvertent production of privileged documents in discovery may be deemed a waiver not only of the privilege as to the specific documents produced, but also as to all other documents addressing the same subject matter. In the context of a joint defense arrangement, where multiple parties have shared privileged materials on overlapping subjects, a single inadvertent production could trigger cascading subject-matter waiver, creating catastrophic exposure for all JDA members. The clawback provision mitigates this risk and provides a procedural framework for addressing inadvertent disclosures promptly and effectively.

9	**[Section 9 --- Government-Investigation Carve-Out]{.underline}**
10	
11	**Classification: Required**
12	
13	**[9.1 Acceptable Position]{.underline}**
14	
15	The JDA must include an **express provision permitting any party to withhold or restrict sharing of materials that are also responsive to a separate government investigation** in which other JDA members are not similarly situated. This carve-out is particularly critical in matters involving parallel proceedings --- a common feature of the antitrust, securities, and environmental litigation contexts in which Vantage frequently operates.
16	
17	The government-investigation carve-out must address the following elements:
18	
19	> **(a) Scope of Covered Investigations.** The carve-out must apply to federal and state criminal investigations, civil investigative demand (\"CID\") proceedings, regulatory inquiry proceedings, formal enforcement actions, and any other form of government investigation, regardless of the agency or authority conducting the investigation.
20	>
21	> **(b) Right to Withhold.** The carve-out must allow the withholding party to decline specific information-sharing requests from the Steering Committee or other JDA members without being deemed in breach of the JDA and without incurring any penalty, adverse inference, or other consequence under the agreement.
22	>
23	> **(c) No Obligation to Disclose the Investigation.** The carve-out must provide that the withholding party is not obligated to disclose the existence or nature of the separate government investigation beyond what is required by applicable law. This is essential because disclosure of the existence of a government investigation may itself be subject to legal restrictions (e.g., grand jury secrecy rules under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 6(e)) and may compromise the withholding party\'s cooperation posture with the investigating authority.
24	
25	**Rationale:** In antitrust matters, DOJ criminal investigations and FTC or state-attorney-general civil investigations frequently proceed in parallel with private litigation. Similarly, in securities and environmental matters, SEC enforcement proceedings and EPA investigations may overlap with civil class actions or multi-district litigation. A party cooperating with a government investigation may face irreconcilable obligations if the JDA compels disclosure of materials also subject to grand jury secrecy, government cooperation agreements, proffer agreements, or similar arrangements. The government-investigation carve-out ensures that Vantage can participate in a joint defense arrangement without jeopardizing its ability to cooperate with --- or respond to --- government proceedings.
26	
27	**[9.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
28	
29	At minimum, the JDA must permit a party to notify the Steering Committee (or all parties, if no steering committee exists) that it is withholding specific materials on grounds of regulatory sensitivity, without requiring identification of the specific investigation or agency involved. This fallback preserves transparency within the joint defense group while protecting the withholding party from the obligation to disclose potentially sensitive details about the nature or source of the government inquiry.
30	
31	The fallback notification should be limited to a statement substantially to the effect of: \"The undersigned party declines to share the requested materials on the ground that they are subject to regulatory sensitivity. No further information regarding the basis for this determination is required under Section \[X\] of this Agreement.\"
32	
33	**[9.3 Never-Accept Term]{.underline}**
34	
35	Any JDA that contains no government-investigation carve-out, or that requires unrestricted sharing of materials irrespective of separate government proceedings, is categorically unacceptable and must be redlined before Vantage will consider execution.
36	
37	Specifically, the following formulations are never-accept terms:
38	
39	> • JDAs that are silent on the topic of parallel government investigations;
40	>
41	> • Provisions requiring \"complete\" or \"unrestricted\" sharing of \"all materials relevant to the defense\";
42	>
43	> • Provisions that obligate a party to disclose the existence, nature, or status of any government investigation as a condition of withholding materials;
44	>
45	> • Provisions that treat a party\'s refusal to share materials on regulatory-sensitivity grounds as a breach of the JDA or a basis for expulsion from the joint defense group.
46	
47	**[Section 10 --- Cost Sharing]{.underline}**
48	
49	**Classification: Preferred**
50	
51	**[10.1 Recommended Position]{.underline}**
52	
53	Joint defense costs --- including joint expert fees, common discovery costs (such as shared document-review platforms, e-discovery vendors, and deposition videography), shared vendor expenses, and joint briefing costs --- should be allocated on a **pro-rata basis determined by each party\'s relative share of the plaintiffs\' claimed damages attributable to that party**, as calculated from the operative complaint or the most recent damages model produced in discovery.
54	
55	This damages-based allocation methodology reflects the principle that each party\'s share of joint defense costs should be proportional to its exposure in the underlying litigation. A party facing a larger share of the claimed damages has a correspondingly greater interest in the joint defense effort and should bear a proportionate share of the costs.
56	
57	Allocations should be **recalculated quarterly** to account for changes in the plaintiffs\' damages theories, amendments to the operative complaint, revisions to expert damages models, and other developments that materially affect the relative exposure of the parties. The recalculation process should be administered by the Steering Committee (if one exists) or by agreement of the parties, with each party having the right to submit updated calculations and supporting data.
58	
59	**[10.2 Fallback Positions]{.underline}**
60	
61	If pro-rata allocation by damages share is not obtainable --- for example, because the damages model does not attribute specific amounts to individual defendants, or because the parties cannot agree on the methodology for calculating relative shares --- Vantage may accept either of the following alternative allocation formulas:
62	
63	> **(a) Equal Pro-Rata Allocation.** Each signatory bears an equal share of joint defense costs (i.e., each party\'s share equals 1/N, where N is the total number of signatories). This approach is simple and transparent but may result in a disproportionate allocation if the parties have materially different levels of exposure.
64	>
65	> **(b) Market-Share Allocation.** Each party\'s share is based on its share of the relevant market as established in the complaint or as determined by available market data. This approach is more closely correlated to exposure than equal allocation but may require negotiation over the definition of the relevant market and the data sources used to calculate market shares.
66	
67	Either fallback is acceptable if pro-rata allocation by damages share is unobtainable.
68	
69	**[10.3 Disfavored Terms]{.underline}**
70	
71	Allocation formulas that assign a disproportionate share of costs to certain parties based on negotiated percentages rather than objective criteria are disfavored. Fixed-percentage splits that do not correlate to any party\'s actual exposure, market share, or other objective measure are disfavored but not Prohibited. Outside counsel should note any such allocation in the review memorandum and recommend an alternative allocation methodology.
72	
73	**[10.4 Audit Rights]{.underline}**
74	
75	Regardless of the allocation formula adopted, the JDA should include a right for any party to audit joint defense expenditures on reasonable notice. The audit right should permit the auditing party (or its designated representative) to review supporting documentation for all expenses charged to the joint defense, including invoices, engagement letters, and fee arrangements with shared vendors and experts. The audit right is a governance safeguard that promotes transparency and accountability and reduces the risk of disputes over cost allocation.
76	
77	**[Section 11 --- Steering Committee]{.underline}**
78	
79	**Classification: Preferred**
80	
81	**[11.1 Recommended Position]{.underline}**
82	
83	If the JDA establishes a Joint Defense Steering Committee or similar governance body (however styled), the committee must provide **equal representation**: each signatory to the JDA receives one seat on the committee, and each seat carries equal voting weight. Equal representation ensures that no single party or subset of parties can dominate the committee\'s decision-making and that all signatories have a direct voice in joint defense strategy, cost allocation, information sharing, and other matters within the committee\'s purview.
84	
85	Alternatively, if equal representation on a committee is impractical due to the large number of signatories, Vantage\'s preferred position is that no steering committee be established at all. In that case, decisions affecting the joint defense should be made by consensus or majority vote of all signatories, with each signatory casting one vote.
86	
87	**[11.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
88	
89	A smaller committee (i.e., one with fewer seats than the total number of signatories) is acceptable, provided that the following conditions are met:
90	
91	> **(a) Rotation.** Seats on the committee rotate among all signatories on a defined schedule (e.g., quarterly or semi-annually). No party may hold a permanent seat, and no party may serve consecutive terms unless all other signatories have had the opportunity to serve.
92	>
93	> **(b) Observer Rights.** Any signatory not then holding a seat on the committee has the right to attend committee meetings as an observer, to receive advance notice of all committee agenda items and proposed actions, and to submit written comments or objections to the committee before any vote is taken.
94	
95	**[11.3 Disfavored Terms]{.underline}**
96	
97	The following committee structures and governance provisions are disfavored and should be avoided where possible:
98	
99	> • Permanent or guaranteed seats for any single party, including the party whose counsel drafted the JDA or the party with the largest market share;
100	>
101	> • Committee structures in which one party or its counsel holds a structural majority of seats or possesses a veto right over committee decisions;
102	>
103	> • Committees in which fewer than all signatories are represented and no rotation mechanism is provided;
104	>
105	> • Committees that have the authority to bind non-member signatories to strategic or financial decisions without a meaningful opportunity for input or objection; and
106	>
107	> • Provisions that delegate to the committee the authority to waive or amend JDA provisions without the consent of all signatories.
108	
109	These structures create a risk that the Steering Committee will be captured by one or more parties with interests that diverge from Vantage\'s, potentially resulting in joint defense decisions that do not serve the Company\'s interests.
110	
111	**[Section 12 --- Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**
112	
113	**Classification: Preferred**
114	
115	**[12.1 Recommended Position]{.underline}**
116	
117	Disputes arising under or in connection with the JDA should be resolved through a two-step process:
118	
119	> **(a) Mandatory Mediation.** As a prerequisite to any binding dispute-resolution mechanism, the disputing parties must engage in good-faith mediation before a neutral mediator mutually agreed upon by the parties. The mediation should be conducted in the city where the underlying litigation is pending and should be completed within thirty (30) days of the date a party provides written notice of a dispute.
120	>
121	> **(b) Litigation in the Forum Court.** If mediation does not resolve the dispute, the parties should submit the dispute to the jurisdiction of the court in which the underlying case is pending. Litigation in the forum court is preferable to arbitration because (i) the forum court is already familiar with the parties, the underlying claims, and the JDA; (ii) the forum court is best positioned to interpret and enforce the JDA\'s privilege-related provisions; and (iii) litigation preserves the right to appeal, which is limited in arbitration.
122	
123	**Application Note:** Where the underlying case is pending in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, JDA disputes should be subject to the jurisdiction of that court.
124	
125	**[12.2 Fallback Positions]{.underline}**
126	
127	> **(a) Arbitration with Mediation Prerequisite.** If arbitration is insisted upon by counterparties, Vantage may accept arbitration only if preceded by mandatory mediation, conducted in the city where the underlying litigation is pending, and administered by a nationally recognized dispute-resolution provider such as the American Arbitration Association (\"AAA\") or JAMS. The arbitration should be conducted before a single arbitrator with experience in complex commercial litigation or the substantive area of the underlying case.
128	>
129	> **(b) Non-Binding Arbitration.** Non-binding arbitration followed by the right to de novo litigation in the forum court is an acceptable intermediate position. This approach provides the benefits of an expedited neutral evaluation while preserving the parties\' right to a full adjudication.
130	
131	**[12.3 Disfavored Terms]{.underline}**
132	
133	The following dispute-resolution provisions are disfavored:
134	
135	> • Binding arbitration as the sole dispute-resolution mechanism without a mediation prerequisite;
136	>
137	> • Arbitration in a venue unrelated to the underlying litigation forum (e.g., arbitration in New York where the underlying case is pending in Illinois);
138	>
139	> • Arbitration under rules that limit discovery or restrict the arbitrator\'s authority to compel production of documents relevant to the JDA dispute;
140	>
141	> • Provisions that require unanimous consent of all JDA members before any signatory may initiate a dispute-resolution proceeding; and
142	>
143	> • Provisions that waive any party\'s right to seek emergency or provisional relief from the forum court pending resolution of the dispute.
144	
145	**[Section 13 --- Post-Settlement Cooperation]{.underline}**
146	
147	**Classification: Preferred**
148	
149	**[13.1 Recommended Position]{.underline}**
150	
151	A settling party\'s obligations to non-settling defendants following settlement should be limited to **preservation of documents** in accordance with applicable litigation-hold obligations. Document preservation is an obligation that typically exists independently of the JDA by operation of law, and incorporating it into the JDA ensures clarity regarding the settling party\'s continuing responsibilities.
152	
153	The JDA should **not** impose an affirmative obligation on a settling party to make witnesses or documents available for depositions, trial testimony, or other litigation activities post-settlement. Once a party has settled and withdrawn from the joint defense, its interests are no longer aligned with those of the non-settling defendants, and the imposition of affirmative cooperation obligations creates friction, ambiguity, and potential liability for the settling party.
154	
155	**[13.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
156	
157	If some cooperation language is unavoidable --- for example, because other signatories insist on a post-settlement cooperation provision as a condition of entry into the JDA --- Vantage may accept a limited obligation to cooperate with document-preservation requests. This obligation should be narrowly defined and should not extend beyond the settling party\'s existing litigation-hold obligations.
158	
159	However, the JDA should not include a **\"commercially reasonable efforts\" witness-availability standard**. This formulation is disfavored because it creates open-ended obligations and significant ambiguity regarding enforcement. The meaning of \"commercially reasonable efforts\" in the context of post-settlement witness availability is inherently uncertain, and disputes over compliance are likely to arise, consuming resources and generating friction among the parties.
160	
161	**[13.3 Disfavored Terms]{.underline}**
162	
163	The following post-settlement cooperation provisions are disfavored and should be resisted in negotiation:
164	
165	> • Affirmative obligations to \"use commercially reasonable efforts\" to make witnesses and documents available for specified periods post-settlement;
166	>
167	> • Obligations to appear at trial or for depositions at the request of non-settling parties;
168	>
169	> • Obligations to provide declarations, affidavits, or other testimonial evidence at the request of non-settling defendants;
170	>
171	> • Any cooperation obligation extending beyond the conclusion of the underlying litigation (including appeals); and
172	>
173	> • Provisions that impose financial penalties or liquidated damages for a settling party\'s failure to comply with post-settlement cooperation obligations.
174	
175	**[Section 14 --- Information-Sharing Scope and Objection Rights]{.underline}**
176	
177	**Classification: Preferred**
178	
179	**[14.1 Recommended Position]{.underline}**
180	
181	The JDA\'s information-sharing provisions are the operational core of the joint defense arrangement and must be drafted with precision. In addition to defining the categories of information to be shared and the mechanics of sharing, the information-sharing provisions must include an **express right for any party to object to or decline specific information-sharing requests** from the Steering Committee or other parties.
182	
183	The grounds for objection must include, at a minimum, the following:
184	
185	> **(a) Work-Product Protection.** A party may decline to share materials that constitute attorney work product prepared for that party\'s individual defense, as distinguished from work product prepared jointly for the benefit of the joint defense group.
186	>
187	> **(b) Separate-Interest Privilege.** A party may decline to share communications or analyses prepared for that party\'s individual defense that are protected by the attorney-client privilege and that were not generated in the course of the joint defense. The \"separate-interest\" privilege protects the party\'s confidential communications with its own counsel regarding matters that, while related to the underlying litigation, involve strategic considerations unique to that party (e.g., settlement strategy, insurance coverage analysis, or potential cross-claims).
188	>
189	> **(c) Regulatory Sensitivity.** A party may decline to share materials relating to government investigations covered by Section 9 of this Playbook, including materials subject to grand jury secrecy, cooperation agreements, proffer agreements, or similar arrangements with government agencies.
190	
191	The objecting party must have a **five (5)-business-day objection window** from receipt of the information-sharing request within which to assert its objection and identify the applicable ground(s). During the objection window, the objecting party is not required to produce the requested materials, and the Steering Committee or requesting party may not take any adverse action based on the objection.
192	
193	**[14.2 Fallback Position]{.underline}**
194	
195	If the five (5)-business-day objection window is not obtainable, Vantage may accept an objection window of no fewer than three (3) business days. The shorter window must still provide a meaningful opportunity for the objecting party to review the request, consult with counsel, and formulate its objection.
196	
197	The substantive grounds for objection --- work product, separate-interest privilege, and regulatory sensitivity --- are non-negotiable in any information-sharing provision. Outside counsel may not agree to an information-sharing mechanism that omits any of these three grounds for objection.
198	
199	**[14.3 Disfavored Terms]{.underline}**
200	
201	The following information-sharing provisions are disfavored and should be resisted in negotiation:
202	
203	> • Information-sharing obligations with no express opt-out or objection right;
204	>
205	> • Mandatory sharing of \"all\" materials relevant to the defense without an objection mechanism;
206	>
207	> • Obligations to share materials within timeframes that do not allow for privilege review (e.g., \"immediately upon request\" or \"within 24 hours\");
208	>
209	> • Provisions that empower the Steering Committee to override an individual party\'s objection by majority vote;
210	>
211	> • Provisions that create an adverse inference or presumption against a party that declines to share materials; and
212	>
213	> • Provisions that require a party to provide a privilege log or detailed description of materials withheld on objection grounds, which could itself disclose privileged information.
214	
215	**[Section 15 --- Additional Standard Terms]{.underline}**
216	
217	**[15.1 No Admission of Liability]{.underline}**
218	
219	**Classification: Required**
220	
221	Every JDA to which Vantage becomes a signatory must include a provision confirming that participation in the joint defense arrangement, execution of the JDA, and the sharing of Joint Defense Materials do not constitute an admission of liability, wrongdoing, or fault by any party. This provision is a standard market term in virtually all JDAs and should not require significant negotiation. The no-admission provision should apply broadly to all proceedings, including the underlying litigation, related matters, government investigations, and any future proceedings. No fallback is needed; if this provision is absent, it must be added.
222	
223	**[15.2 Confidentiality Markings]{.underline}**
224	
225	**Classification: Preferred**
226	
227	Shared materials should bear a marking such as **\"Joint Defense Material --- Privileged and Confidential\"** or an equivalent designation. The purpose of the marking is to provide a visual reminder that the materials are subject to the JDA\'s confidentiality provisions and to the common-interest privilege, reducing the risk of inadvertent disclosure or mishandling. The specific formulation of the marking may vary, but it should clearly identify the materials as joint defense materials subject to privilege protection. Outside counsel should ensure that Vantage\'s internal document-management protocols are configured to apply the agreed-upon marking to all materials shared under the JDA.
228	
229	**[15.3 Limitation of Liability]{.underline}**
230	
231	**Classification: Preferred**
232	
233	Where available, the JDA should include a mutual limitation-of-liability clause among JDA parties for breaches of the agreement. The limitation should cap each party\'s liability for breach at a reasonable amount (e.g., the party\'s aggregate cost-sharing contributions under the JDA or a fixed dollar amount) and should exclude from the cap any liability arising from willful or intentional breaches, including intentional disclosure of Joint Defense Materials to unauthorized third parties.
234	
235	This provision is not commonly included in all JDAs, and its absence is not a basis for declining to execute an otherwise acceptable agreement. However, where Vantage has the opportunity to negotiate a limitation-of-liability provision, it should seek to do so.
236	
237	**[15.4 Amendment and Waiver]{.underline}**
238	
239	**Classification: Preferred**
240	
241	The JDA should require **unanimous written consent of all signatories** for any amendment or waiver of any provision of the agreement. This ensures that no party\'s rights under the JDA can be modified without its affirmative consent and prevents a majority of signatories from altering the terms of the arrangement to the detriment of a minority. The amendment-and-waiver provision should specify that waivers must be in writing, that a waiver of one provision does not constitute a waiver of any other provision, and that a waiver on one occasion does not constitute a waiver on any subsequent occasion.
242	
243	**[Section 16 --- Review and Approval Process]{.underline}**
244	
245	**[16.1 Written Assessment]{.underline}**
246	
247	Outside counsel retained by Vantage on any matter in which a JDA is proposed must prepare a written assessment comparing each material provision of the proposed JDA against the corresponding standard in this Playbook. The written assessment must identify, for each material provision:
248	
249	> **(a)** Provisions that satisfy the applicable Required, Preferred, or Prohibited standard, with a brief notation confirming compliance;
250	>
251	> **(b)** Provisions that deviate from a Preferred standard, with an explanation of the nature and extent of the deviation and a recommended response (accept, negotiate, or reject);
252	>
253	> **(c)** Provisions that fail to satisfy a Required standard, with a description of the deficiency, the risk associated with the deficiency, and the specific revisions needed to bring the provision into conformity; and
254	>
255	> **(d)** Provisions that contain a Prohibited (never-accept) term, with identification of the specific language at issue and a recommended redline to remove or replace it.
256	
257	The written assessment should be organized to follow the structure of this Playbook (Sections 3 through 15) and should address each topic area, even if the proposed JDA is silent on a particular topic. Silence on a Required topic (e.g., omission of a clawback provision) is itself a deficiency that must be identified and addressed.
258	
259	**[16.2 Redlined JDA]{.underline}**
260	
261	A redlined version of the proposed JDA reflecting all changes necessary to bring it into conformity with Required and Prohibited standards must accompany the written assessment. The redline should also include recommended changes to address Preferred standards, clearly distinguished from Required changes so that the General Counsel can assess the relative priority of each proposed revision. Outside counsel should use tracked changes to prepare the redline and should include comments or annotations explaining the basis for each proposed change.
262	
263	**[16.3 Submission to General Counsel]{.underline}**
264	
265	Both the written assessment and the redlined JDA must be submitted to the General Counsel (or his designee) for review and approval before any response is communicated to the proponent of the JDA or to other co-defendants. Outside counsel may not circulate a counterproposal, redline, or other response to the proposed JDA until the General Counsel has reviewed and approved the submission.
266	
267	The General Counsel will review the submission, consult with outside counsel as needed, and either (i) approve the proposed response for circulation, (ii) direct revisions to the response, or (iii) determine that Vantage should decline to participate in the JDA. The General Counsel\'s decision will be communicated to outside counsel in writing.
268	
269	**[16.4 Execution Authority]{.underline}**
270	
271	Execution authority for JDAs rests solely with the General Counsel or an officer designated in writing by the General Counsel. No other officer, employee, or agent of Vantage is authorized to execute a JDA on the Company\'s behalf. Outside counsel are not authorized to execute JDAs on Vantage\'s behalf unless they have received a specific written authorization from the General Counsel for the particular JDA in question.
